1.prompt: The stone you laid today — where did it come from?
options: From the quarry across the valley
From the burnt ruins of the city itself
It came by cart, with the man from the capital
1.note: From the ruins. The city is put back together out of its own material, which is why clearing rubble and laying stone are one job in two stages.

2.prompt: Two residents told you different things about the road. How does the game show you which one is right?
options: By the colour of the name above their head
It doesn't
By the icon that appears on the line
2.note: It doesn't, and it isn't going to. You decide with what you have: who saw it, where they saw it from, and what being wrong costs in each of the two directions.

options: the other side gives up
the other side is cut down
your strength runs out
3.note: It ends when somebody gives up. Nobody counts the fallen on this wall, on your side or theirs: the watch exists so the attack isn't worth making.

4.prompt: At today's roll call, how were the stretches handed out?
options: By lot, so nobody could complain
Each person took the piece in front of their own house
The best masons took the worst stretches
4.note: Each one close to home. It is the most obvious division and the hardest to cheat: nobody has to be watched to build the wall outside their own door properly.

5.prompt: The two men shouted from the road all day. Which move answers that?
options: Patrol
A heavier watch
None of them
5.note: None of them. The season's first threat is the only one with no counter: it goes away when the wall goes up in front of it. Morale lost to talk costs the talker nothing.

6.prompt: Half and half turned up in the middle of the standoff. What does that move do?
options: Everyone works and watches at the same time
Half the city leaves and half stays
It doubles the load on whoever was already laying stone
6.note: Both things in the same person, at the same time. It is the strongest move because it is the only one that does not choose between the work and the defence, and the other side had no answer ready for it.

7.prompt: That day the city did two things. Which two?
options: Prayed, and posted a guard the next day
Prayed and posted a guard, on the same day
Posted a guard, and left the praying for when there was time
7.note: Both, with an "and" in the middle. It is the axis of the whole season: prayer alone loses the wall, a guard alone loses the reason to raise it.

8.prompt: Five letters arrived. What tells a true letter from a well-written one?
options: Who delivered it
The seal
Whether it matches what was already written
8.note: Checking it against what was already written. A guard is no use against paper; against paper what works is having the earlier version to hand and comparing the two.

9.prompt: The name of whoever repaired each stretch was written down. What for?
options: So it is known whose hands did which piece
So each of them could be paid for the work
So the next person in charge could be chosen
9.note: For the record. The list of who raised this wall is the only place most of these people appear at all: forty-odd names, each with a trade beside it, and nothing else.
